title: Engineering with Foundation Models
subtitle: Choose, understand, evaluate and steer foundation models like an engineer: scale and serving arithmetic, transformer internals, rigorous model and system evaluation, LLM judges in CI, and prompt optimisation.
outcomes: Explain what makes a foundation model, how scale drives its abilities, and estimate training, inference and memory costs
Explain self-attention, tokenisation, context windows and the KV cache, and what quantisation trades away
Compare and select foundation models against an application's requirements
Evaluate models with benchmarks, reference metrics and human ratings, with agreement and confidence intervals
Build and validate AI-as-a-judge pipelines and run them as quality gates in CI/CD
Optimise prompts with held-out evaluation, and choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning
prerequisites: Applied Machine Learning with TensorFlow, or experience training and evaluating models in Python; Transformers and Large Language Models helps with module 2, and Prompting and LLM Application Design with modules 4 and 5. Install Python 3.10+ and pip install numpy scipy scikit-learn statsmodels nltk pydantic pytest anthropic. Labs run without an API key; the capstone needs a Claude Console API key with credit and CLAUDE_MODEL set to a current model ID.
description:
Foundation models are general-purpose engines: trained once on broad data, then adapted to thousands of tasks. Engineering with them means making decisions that hold up under scrutiny: which model to use and where to run it, what its context window and memory footprint really cost, how to tell whether it's good enough, and how to keep it good as prompts, models and data change. This course works through those decisions. You'll start with what scale does and doesn't buy, and how to shortlist models against requirements; go inside the transformer to see what attention, tokenisers, the KV cache and quantisation mean for cost and quality; then spend two modules on evaluation, from benchmarks, BLEU and ROUGE and properly run human ratings to AI-as-a-judge pipelines that are validated against people and run as quality gates in CI/CD. The last module treats prompt engineering as experimentation, and sets it beside retrieval and fine-tuning.

Every module has a hands-on Python lab that runs on an ordinary laptop without an API key: scaling arithmetic and a model shortlist, attention, byte-pair encoding and quantisation in NumPy, metrics against human ratings, judge validation with a pytest quality gate, and prompt selection with paired statistical tests. The capstone is an automated evaluation pipeline for a customer support chatbot, with your own rubric, test set and judge.

modules.title: Introduction to Foundation Models
modules.summary: What foundation models are, how they're trained and adapted, what scaling laws and emergent abilities tell an engineer, and how to shortlist models for an application.

lessons.title: What makes a model a foundation model
objectives: Define foundation models and self-supervised pretraining
Describe the ways a pretrained model is adapted to a task
key_points: The term foundation model was popularised by a 2021 report from Stanford's Center for Research on Foundation Models, for models trained on broad data, usually with self-supervision at scale, that can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks.

Self-supervised pretraining needs no human labels: the training signal comes from the data itself, such as predicting the next token of text or a hidden patch of an image, which is what makes training on vast unlabelled collections possible.

One pretrained model can be adapted in several ways: prompting with instructions and examples, retrieving relevant data at query time, fine-tuning on task data, or connecting tools. Most applications start with prompting and retrieval before considering fine-tuning.
Foundation models now cover text, code, images, audio and video, and many are multimodal, accepting several kinds of input in one model.

Because many applications are built on a few models, those models' strengths, biases and failure modes spread to everything built on them, which the report called homogenisation: evaluate each application, not only the model.

lessons.title: Scale: parameters, data and compute
objectives: Explain what scaling laws say about loss, parameters, data and compute
Estimate training and inference compute with standard approximations
key_points: Scaling-law studies found that a language model's loss falls smoothly, roughly as a power law, as parameters, training data and compute grow, provided none of them is the bottleneck (Kaplan and colleagues, 2020).

Training a dense transformer takes about 6 × N × D floating-point operations for N parameters and D training tokens, and generating takes about 2 × N per token; these approximations let you compare costs before running anything.

The 2022 Chinchilla study (Hoffmann and colleagues) found that, for a fixed compute budget, parameters and training tokens should grow in roughly equal proportion, about 20 tokens per parameter, and that earlier large models were undertrained by that measure.
Many recent models are trained on far more tokens than compute-optimal, because a smaller model trained for longer is cheaper to serve, and serving costs dominate for a model that many people use.
Scale improves average performance, not everything at once: some tasks plateau, and smaller models trained on well-chosen data can beat larger ones on particular tasks, so measure on your own task.

lessons.title: Emergent abilities, and the debate about them
objectives: Describe in-context learning and emergent abilities
Explain why the evidence for sudden emergence is debated, and what it means for model choice
key_points: In-context learning, doing a new task from instructions and a few examples in the prompt without any weight updates, was the headline finding of the 2020 GPT-3 paper (Brown and colleagues), and it improved markedly with model size.

Wei and colleagues (2022) described emergent abilities: abilities near chance in smaller models that appear well above chance only past a certain scale, such as some multi-step arithmetic and reasoning tasks.

Schaeffer and colleagues (2023) argued that many apparent jumps come from all-or-nothing metrics such as exact match, and that smoother metrics, such as per-token accuracy, often show gradual improvement.

Either way, the practical lesson is the same: abilities can differ sharply between model sizes, so don't assume a smaller or cheaper model can do what a larger one does; test it on your task with the metric you care about.

lessons.title: Choosing a foundation model
objectives: Turn an application's requirements into filters and weighted criteria
Compare API and open-weight models, including licensing and operations
key_points: Start from requirements, not leaderboards: the task and its quality bar, input and output lengths, languages, modalities, latency and throughput targets, cost per request, and constraints on data, deployment and licensing.

API models are quick to adopt and are run and updated by the provider; open-weight models can run on your own infrastructure, which helps with data control and customisation but makes you responsible for serving, scaling and updates.
Open-weight licences vary: some are permissive, such as Apache 2.0, while others restrict commercial use or add conditions, so read the licence before choosing a model.

Treat must-haves, such as a minimum context window or data staying in a region, as filters; then compare what's left on quality measured with your own evaluation set, cost and latency, and choose the smallest model that meets the bar.
Model versions change and are retired, so pin the version you evaluated, keep the evaluation set for testing replacements, and design your code so the model can be swapped.

modules.title: Inside Foundation Models
modules.summary: The parts of the transformer that decide what models cost and how they behave: attention, tokenisation, pretraining and context windows, the KV cache, and the basics of serving and quantisation.

lessons.title: Self-attention for engineers
objectives: Explain how scaled dot-product attention and causal masking work
Explain why attention's cost grows with the square of the sequence length
key_points: Self-attention computes, for each token, a weighted average of value vectors from the tokens it can see; the weights are the softmax of its query's dot products with their keys, divided by the square root of the key dimension: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V.

Decoder-only models, used for most generative LLMs, apply a causal mask so each token attends only to itself and earlier tokens, which is what lets them generate left to right. Encoder models such as BERT attend in both directions and suit embeddings and classification.
Multi-head attention runs several attention operations in parallel on smaller projections and concatenates the results, so different heads can track different relationships.

The matrix of attention scores has an entry for every pair of tokens, so its compute and memory grow with the square of the sequence length: doubling the context quadruples it, one reason long contexts cost more.

A transformer block wraps attention with a feed-forward network, residual connections and normalisation, and models stack dozens of blocks; position information comes from positional encodings such as rotary embeddings (RoPE).

lessons.title: Tokenisation and what it costs
objectives: Explain how byte-pair encoding builds a vocabulary
Explain how tokenisation affects cost, context use and some model failures
key_points: Most LLMs use subword tokenisers, such as byte-pair encoding (BPE), WordPiece or SentencePiece's unigram model, which keep common words whole and split rare ones into pieces, so any text can be encoded with a fixed vocabulary.

BPE starts from characters or bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary reaches its target size; byte-level BPE can encode any input without unknown tokens.

A larger vocabulary shortens sequences, saving context and compute, but enlarges the embedding and output layers; languages and scripts under-represented in the tokeniser's training data split into more tokens, so they cost more to process.

Token counts are model-specific: limits and prices are in that model's tokens, so count with the provider's own tool, such as the Claude API's token-counting endpoint, rather than another model's tokeniser.

Tokenisation explains some odd failures: models can struggle to count letters or reverse words because they see tokens rather than characters, and numbers split inconsistently, which can hurt arithmetic.

lessons.title: Pretraining, context windows and the KV cache
objectives: Explain the pretraining objective and perplexity
Explain context windows, long-context limitations and the KV cache
key_points: Pretraining minimises the cross-entropy of next-token predictions over a huge corpus; perplexity, the exponential of the average cross-entropy, measures how well a model predicts held-out text, and lower is better.
The context window is the maximum number of tokens, prompt and output together, the model can attend to in one request; anything longer must be truncated, summarised or retrieved selectively.
A long window isn't used evenly: 'Lost in the Middle' (Liu and colleagues, 2023) found that models used information at the start and end of long inputs more reliably than information in the middle.

During generation, the keys and values of earlier tokens are kept in a KV cache so each new token needs only its own projections; the cache grows linearly with length, at about 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × tokens × bytes per value.

Grouped-query attention shares keys and values across groups of query heads to shrink the KV cache, and prefix caching reuses the cached keys and values of a repeated prompt prefix, saving compute on repeated prompts.

lessons.title: Serving and quantisation basics
objectives: Estimate the memory a model needs at different precisions
Explain how quantisation works and what it trades away
Name the measurements that matter when serving a model
key_points: Weights need about parameters × bytes per parameter: 4 bytes in fp32, 2 in fp16 or bf16, 1 in int8 and half a byte in 4-bit formats, so a 7-billion-parameter model needs about 14 GB in bf16 before the KV cache and activations.

Quantisation stores weights in fewer bits plus scale factors: absmax int8 divides each group of weights by its largest absolute value over 127 and rounds. Smaller groups, such as one scale per row, keep errors lower, especially when a few outlier weights would otherwise set the scale.

Lower precision saves memory and often speeds up inference, at a cost in quality that grows as bits shrink and varies by task, so evaluate a quantised model on your own tasks. GPTQ and AWQ are common methods, and GGUF is the format llama.cpp uses.
Serving engines such as vLLM and SGLang batch requests continuously and manage the KV cache efficiently to raise throughput; Ollama and llama.cpp run quantised models on a laptop.

Measure serving with time to first token, time per output token, throughput in tokens per second and tail latency under realistic concurrency, because batching raises throughput but can slow each request.

"""Scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask, in NumPy, on a six-token toy sequence.

Run: python attention.py
"""

import numpy as np

TOKENS = ["The", "room", "is", "booked", "until", "noon"]


def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)


def attention(Q, K, V, causal=True):
    """softmax(Q K^T / sqrt(d)) V. With causal=True each position sees only itself and earlier positions."""
    d = Q.shape[-1]
    # TODO 1: compute the scores Q @ K^T divided by sqrt(d) (K.swapaxes(-1, -2) transposes the last two axes)
    scores = np.zeros((Q.shape[-2], K.shape[-2]))
    if causal:
        # TODO 2: set the scores above the diagonal to -inf (np.triu(np.ones((n, n), dtype=bool), k=1)
        #         marks them), so the softmax gives them zero weight
        pass
    weights = softmax(scores)
    return weights @ V, weights


def main():
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    d_model, n_heads = 8, 2
    X = rng.normal(size=(len(TOKENS), d_model))  # one (made-up) embedding per token
    Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_model)) / np.sqrt(d_model) for _ in range(3))
    out, w = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)
    print("Attention weights (row = query token, column = key token):")
    for token, row in zip(TOKENS, w):
        print(f"  {token:<7}" + " ".join(f"{v:4.2f}" for v in row))
    print("Rows sum to 1:", bool(np.allclose(w.sum(axis=1), 1)), "| nothing above the diagonal:",
          bool(np.all(np.triu(w, k=1) == 0)))
    # Multi-head: split the 8 dimensions into 2 heads of 4, attend in each, and join the results.
    split = lambda M: M.reshape(len(TOKENS), n_heads, d_model // n_heads).transpose(1, 0, 2)
    heads, _ = attention(split(X @ Wq), split(X @ Wk), split(X @ Wv))
    joined = heads.transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(len(TOKENS), d_model)
    print("Output shape:", out.shape, "| per-head output shape:", heads.shape, "| joined:", joined.shape)
    for n in (1024, 2048, 4096):
        print(f"{n} tokens: {n * n:,} attention scores per head per layer")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Memory arithmetic and absmax quantisation of a weight matrix, per tensor and per row.

Run: python quantise.py
"""

import numpy as np

BYTES = {"fp32": 4, "bf16": 2, "int8": 1, "int4": 0.5}


def weights_gb(params, fmt):
    return params * BYTES[fmt] / 1e9


def kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, tokens, bytes_per_value=2):
    """Keys and values (the 2) for every layer, KV head, dimension and token."""
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * tokens * bytes_per_value


def quantise(W, bits, per_row):
    """Symmetric absmax quantisation: scale = max|w| / qmax, q = round(w / scale), clipped to +-qmax."""
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1  # 127 for int8, 7 for int4
    # TODO 1: compute the scale from the largest absolute value, over each row (axis=1, keepdims=True)
    #         when per_row is True or over the whole matrix otherwise, then round and clip
    raise NotImplementedError
    return q.astype(np.int8), scale


def relative_error(a, b):
    return float(np.linalg.norm(a - b) / np.linalg.norm(a))


def main():
    for name, n in (("7B", 7e9), ("70B", 70e9)):
        print(f"{name} weights: " + ", ".join(f"{fmt} {weights_gb(n, fmt):.1f} GB" for fmt in BYTES))
    gqa = kv_cache_bytes(layers=32, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128, tokens=8192)
    full = kv_cache_bytes(layers=32, kv_heads=32, head_dim=128, tokens=8192)
    print(f"KV cache for 8,192 tokens, 32 layers, head size 128, bf16: {gqa / 2**30:.2f} GiB with 8 KV heads, "
          f"{full / 2**30:.2f} GiB with 32")
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
    W = rng.normal(0, 0.02, size=(256, 256))
    W[3, 7] = 0.9  # a single outlier weight, as real models often have
    x = rng.normal(size=256)
    for bits in (8, 4):
        for per_row in (False, True):
            q, scale = quantise(W, bits, per_row)
            W_hat = q * scale
            label = "per row   " if per_row else "per tensor"
            print(f"int{bits} {label}: weight error {relative_error(W, W_hat):.4f}, "
                  f"output error {relative_error(W @ x, W_hat @ x):.4f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: np.exp(-np.inf) is 0, which is why masking with -inf gives masked positions zero weight.
If your BPE merges differ, check the tie-break: equal counts must go to the pair that sorts first.
In quantise(), np.abs(W).max(axis=1, keepdims=True) keeps one scale per row in a shape that broadcasts against W.

modules.title: Model Evaluation
modules.summary: Why evaluating generation is hard, what benchmarks can and can't tell you, where BLEU and ROUGE mislead, and how to run human evaluation with agreement measures and confidence intervals.

lessons.title: Why evaluating generation is hard
objectives: Explain why generative outputs are harder to evaluate than classifications
Turn open-ended tasks into checkable ones, including pass@k for code
key_points: A classifier's output is right or wrong, but a generated answer can be correct in many wordings and wrong in subtle ways, so there's rarely a single reference to compare with.
Quality has several dimensions, such as correctness, faithfulness to sources, completeness, helpfulness, style and safety, which can conflict and need separate measures.
Outputs vary between runs, so evaluate over many cases, repeat important comparisons, and report uncertainty rather than a single number.
Where you can, make open tasks checkable: multiple-choice questions, exact match on an extracted final answer, unit tests for generated code, or schema checks for structured output.
For code, pass@k estimates the chance that at least one of k samples passes the tests; with n samples of which c pass, the unbiased estimate is 1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k).

lessons.title: Benchmarks: what MMLU and others tell you
objectives: Describe common benchmarks and what they measure
Explain contamination, saturation and set-up sensitivity
key_points: Benchmarks give a common yardstick: MMLU tests knowledge with multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects, GSM8K tests grade-school maths word problems, and HumanEval tests Python functions against unit tests.

Contamination, where test items or close copies appear in training data, inflates scores; and as models improve, benchmarks saturate near their ceiling and stop separating them, so harder successors such as MMLU-Pro appear.

Scores depend on the set-up, such as the number of examples in the prompt, the prompt format, how answers are extracted and whether reasoning is allowed, so compare only numbers measured the same way.
A benchmark measures its own tasks, not yours: use public results to build a shortlist, and an evaluation set built from your real inputs to decide.

lessons.title: Reference-based metrics: BLEU, ROUGE and their limits
objectives: Explain how BLEU and ROUGE are computed
Recognise when overlap metrics mislead
key_points: BLEU, designed in 2002 for machine translation, combines modified n-gram precisions for 1- to 4-grams by geometric mean, with a brevity penalty for short outputs; it was meant for a whole test set, and single sentences need smoothing.
ROUGE, designed for summarisation, measures n-gram overlap with references with an emphasis on recall: ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 count unigrams and bigrams, and ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence.
Overlap metrics reward surface similarity: they penalise correct paraphrases, and they can score an answer highly when one changed word, such as a date or a 'not', makes it wrong.

Embedding-based metrics such as BERTScore capture paraphrase better than n-grams, but none of these checks facts, so use them to track regressions on narrow tasks with good references, alongside checks that do.

lessons.title: Human evaluation done properly
objectives: Design a human evaluation with a rubric, blinding and several raters
Measure inter-rater agreement and the uncertainty of a comparison
key_points: Human judgement is the reference standard for qualities like helpfulness and tone, but it's slow and expensive, so use it to validate automatic measures and for decisions that matter.
Give raters a rubric with anchored levels and examples, hide which system produced each output, randomise the order, and have several raters score at least part of the data.

Pairwise comparisons, asking which of two outputs is better, are often more reliable than absolute scores, and many pairwise votes can be turned into a ranking with an Elo or Bradley-Terry model, as public chatbot leaderboards do.

Measure inter-rater agreement: Cohen's kappa corrects two raters' agreement for chance, and a weighted kappa gives partial credit on ordinal scales; low agreement means the rubric or the task needs work before the scores can be trusted.
Report uncertainty: a bootstrap confidence interval, from resampling the cases with replacement, shows whether a difference between systems is larger than the noise.

"""Reference-based metrics against human ratings: ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L and BLEU, rater agreement, a bootstrap
confidence interval and pass@k.

Run: python metrics.py   (needs pip install nltk scipy scikit-learn numpy)
"""

import json
import re
from math import comb

import numpy as np
from nltk.translate.bleu_score import SmoothingFunction, sentence_bleu
from scipy.stats import spearmanr
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score


def words(text):
    return re.findall(r"\w+", text.lower())


def f1(overlap, n_candidate, n_reference):
    if overlap == 0:
        return 0.0
    precision, recall = overlap / n_candidate, overlap / n_reference
    return 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)


def rouge1(candidate, reference):
    """Unigram overlap F1 (each word counted at most as often as it appears in both)."""
    c, r = words(candidate), words(reference)
    # TODO 1: count the overlapping words: for each distinct word, the smaller of its counts in c and r
    #         (collections.Counter's & operator does this), then return f1(overlap, len(c), len(r))
    raise NotImplementedError


def lcs_length(a, b):
    """Length of the longest common subsequence of two word lists (dynamic programming)."""
    table = [[0] * (len(b) + 1) for _ in range(len(a) + 1)]
    for i, x in enumerate(a, 1):
        for j, y in enumerate(b, 1):
            # TODO 2: if the words match, extend the diagonal (table[i-1][j-1] + 1); otherwise take the larger
            #         of table[i-1][j] and table[i][j-1]
            pass
    return table[-1][-1]


def rouge_l(candidate, reference):
    c, r = words(candidate), words(reference)
    return f1(lcs_length(c, r), len(c), len(r))


def bleu(candidate, reference):
    """Sentence BLEU (1- to 4-grams) with smoothing, which single sentences need."""
    return sentence_bleu([words(reference)], words(candidate), smoothing_function=SmoothingFunction().method1)


def pass_at_k(n, c, k):
    """Unbiased pass@k: the chance that at least one of k samples, from n with c correct, passes."""
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)


def bootstrap_ci(diffs, n_resamples=10_000, seed=0):
    """95% percentile bootstrap interval for the mean of paired differences."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    diffs = np.asarray(diffs, dtype=float)
    # TODO 3: draw n_resamples samples of len(diffs) indices with replacement (rng.integers), take the
    #         mean of each resample, and return the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
    return (0.0, 0.0)


def main():
    with open("summaries.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        items = json.load(f)["items"]
    metric_l, human, r1, r2 = [], [], [], []
    print(f"{'item':<5}{'sys':<4}{'ROUGE-1':>8}{'ROUGE-L':>8}{'BLEU':>7}{'human':>7}")
    for it in items:
        for system in ("A", "B"):
            text = it[system]
            mean_human = (it["rater1"][system] + it["rater2"][system]) / 2
            metric_l.append(rouge_l(text, it["reference"]))
            human.append(mean_human)
            r1.append(it["rater1"][system])
            r2.append(it["rater2"][system])
            print(f"{it['id']:<5}{system:<4}{rouge1(text, it['reference']):>8.2f}{metric_l[-1]:>8.2f}"
                  f"{bleu(text, it['reference']):>7.2f}{mean_human:>7.1f}")
    for system, offset in (("A", 0), ("B", 1)):
        print(f"System {system}: mean ROUGE-L {np.mean(metric_l[offset::2]):.2f}, mean human score {np.mean(human[offset::2]):.2f}")
    rho, _ = spearmanr(metric_l, human)
    print(f"Spearman correlation of ROUGE-L with human scores: {rho:.2f}")
    print(f"Cohen's kappa between raters: {cohen_kappa_score(r1, r2):.2f} unweighted, "
          f"{cohen_kappa_score(r1, r2, weights='quadratic'):.2f} quadratic-weighted")
    diffs = [h_b - h_a for h_a, h_b in zip(human[0::2], human[1::2])]
    low, high = bootstrap_ci(diffs)
    print(f"Human score, B minus A: mean {np.mean(diffs):.2f}, 95% bootstrap CI {low:.2f} to {high:.2f}")
    print(f"pass@1 = {pass_at_k(10, 3, 1):.3f}, pass@5 = {pass_at_k(10, 3, 5):.3f} (10 samples, 3 pass the tests)")

    main()

modules.title: System Evaluation
modules.summary: Evaluate the whole application, not just the model: realistic test sets, component checks, AI-as-a-judge pipelines validated against human labels and tested for bias, and evaluation as an automated gate in CI/CD.

lessons.title: From model evaluation to system evaluation
objectives: Explain why an application needs end-to-end and component-level evaluation
Build an evaluation set from real usage and slice its results
key_points: Users experience a system, not a model: prompts, retrieval, tools, business rules and the interface all shape each result, so evaluate the system end to end on realistic inputs.
Evaluate components too, so failures can be located: retrieval recall, tool-call correctness, parsing success and guardrail decisions each have their own checks.

Build the evaluation set from real usage where you can, with consent and personal data removed, plus edge cases, adversarial inputs and past incidents, and record what a good response must do for each.
Slice results by segment, such as intent, language or customer type, because an average can hide a segment that fails; and keep a held-out set that isn't used while tuning.
Track cost and latency alongside quality for every version, because a change that improves quality may be too slow or too expensive to ship.

lessons.title: AI-as-a-judge: design
objectives: Design pointwise, pairwise and reference-guided LLM judges
Write judging criteria and structured verdicts that can be audited
key_points: An LLM judge evaluates outputs against written criteria: pointwise (score one output), pairwise (choose the better of two) or reference-guided (compare with a gold answer).
Write criteria a person could apply consistently: define each one, such as accuracy against the knowledge base, tone and helpfulness, with what passes and what fails and an example of each.
Pass or fail judgements on one criterion at a time are more reliable than one overall score out of 10; give the judge the material it needs, such as the article and the customer's question.
Ask for a short reason before the verdict, and return the verdict as structured output with a fixed schema, so it can be parsed and audited.
Use a strong model as the judge, ideally from a different family from the model being judged, and keep the judge's model version and prompt fixed while comparing systems.

lessons.title: Validating and de-biasing the judge
objectives: Validate an LLM judge against human labels
Detect and counter position and verbosity bias
key_points: Before trusting a judge, compare its verdicts with careful human labels on a sample of a few dozen or more outputs: report agreement, Cohen's kappa and the confusion matrix for each criterion.

Known biases include position bias (preferring the first or second answer in a pair), verbosity bias (preferring longer answers) and self-preference (favouring outputs like its own); Zheng and colleagues documented them in 2023 when introducing MT-Bench.
Counter position bias by judging each pair in both orders and counting only consistent verdicts; counter verbosity bias with criteria that penalise padding and by comparing answers of similar length.
Read the disagreements: they show which criteria the judge misreads, which you fix in its prompt or rubric before validating again.
Validate again whenever the judge's model, its prompt or the kind of output changes, and keep a small human-labelled set for regular spot checks.

lessons.title: Automating evaluation in CI/CD
objectives: Run evaluations as automated tests with thresholds
Detect regressions without failing on noise
key_points: Treat evaluations as tests: run them automatically when prompts, models, retrieval settings or code change, and block a release that falls below agreed thresholds.
Use tiers: fast deterministic checks on every commit, a larger judged suite on pull requests or nightly, and human review for releases or high-risk changes.
Compare with a stored baseline as well as an absolute bar, and flag a regression only when the drop is larger than run-to-run noise, using a significance test, confidence intervals or repeated runs.
Store each run's results with the versions of the prompt, model, data and judge, so any score can be reproduced and explained.
Keep API keys in the CI system's secrets, cache model outputs keyed by their exact inputs to save cost, and set a spending budget for each run.

"""An LLM judge for a support chatbot: the prompt, a structured verdict, and validation against human labels,
including a position-bias test for pairwise judging.

Offline it reads recorded verdicts from judge_data.json. call_judge() shows how to get a verdict from the API.
Run: python judge.py
"""

import json
from typing import Literal

from pydantic import BaseModel
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score, confusion_matrix

JUDGE_PROMPT = """You are grading one answer from a broadband provider's support chatbot on a single criterion.
<criterion name="{name}">{definition}</criterion>
<article>{article}</article>
<question>{question}</question>
<answer>{answer}</answer>
Think about the criterion only. Give a one-sentence reason first, then the verdict: pass or fail."""


class Verdict(BaseModel):
    reason: str  # first, so the verdict follows the reasoning
    verdict: Literal["pass", "fail"]


def load(path="judge_data.json"):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        return json.load(f)


def judge_vs_human(items):
    """Agreement, Cohen's kappa and the confusion matrix (rows: human pass/fail; columns: judge pass/fail)."""
    human = [it["human"] for it in items]
    judge = [Verdict.model_validate_json(it["judge"]).verdict for it in items]
    # TODO 1: return the share of items where the two agree, cohen_kappa_score(human, judge), and
    #         confusion_matrix(human, judge, labels=["pass", "fail"])
    raise NotImplementedError


def position_bias(pairs):
    """Each pair was judged twice: with A shown first ('ab') and with B shown first ('ba'). The verdict names
    the answer chosen. Returns (consistent pairs, verdicts that chose whichever answer was shown first)."""
    # TODO 2: count the pairs whose two verdicts agree, and the verdicts that chose the first-shown
    #         answer (A in the 'ab' order, B in the 'ba' order)
    raise NotImplementedError


def call_judge(name, definition, article, question, answer):
    """The only function that talks to the API: one criterion, structured output."""
    import os

    import anthropic

    client = anthropic.Anthropic()
    prompt = JUDGE_PROMPT.format(name=name, definition=definition, article=article, question=question, answer=answer)
    response = client.messages.parse(model=os.environ["CLAUDE_MODEL"], max_tokens=1024,
                                     messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], output_format=Verdict)
    return response.parsed_output


def main():
    data = load()
    agreement, kappa, matrix = judge_vs_human(data["items"])
    print(f"Accuracy judge vs human labels: agreement {agreement:.2f}, Cohen's kappa {kappa:.2f}")
    print(f"Confusion matrix (rows human pass/fail, columns judge pass/fail): {matrix.tolist()}")
    lenient = [it["id"] for it in data["items"]
               if it["human"] == "fail" and Verdict.model_validate_json(it["judge"]).verdict == "pass"]
    print("Judge passed answers the human failed:", ", ".join(lenient))
    consistent, first = position_bias(data["pairs"])
    n = len(data["pairs"])
    print(f"Pairwise: consistent in both orders {consistent}/{n}; chose the first-shown answer in {first} of "
          f"{2 * n} verdicts ({first / (2 * n):.2f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.summary: Prompting as engineering: reasoning on demand, examples and system prompts at scale, designs that reduce hallucination, prompt optimisation that survives held-out testing, and when to retrieve or fine-tune instead.

lessons.title: Reasoning on demand: chain-of-thought and thinking modes
objectives: Decide when to ask for reasoning and how to evaluate it
Weigh the accuracy, cost and latency of reasoning settings
key_points: Chain-of-thought prompting has the model write out its reasoning before answering, which improves multi-step problems; it's easiest to evaluate when the final answer goes in a separate, parseable field.

Models with built-in reasoning, such as Claude's extended thinking, reason before replying without being asked; prompting for steps then adds less, and high-level guidance about what to consider tends to work better than prescribing the steps.
Reasoning costs output tokens and time, so treat its depth as a setting to tune: compare accuracy, cost and latency at different levels on your evaluation set.
Reasoning text can be unfaithful, leaving out what actually drove the answer (Turpin and colleagues, 2023), so judge outputs by their results, not by how plausible the reasoning sounds.

lessons.title: Examples and system prompts at scale
objectives: Use many-shot prompting and example selection deliberately
Keep system prompts stable, cacheable and testable
key_points: With long context windows, many-shot prompting, with dozens or hundreds of examples, can keep improving results on some tasks (Agarwal and colleagues, 2024), at an input-token cost that prompt caching can reduce.

The choice and order of examples can change results noticeably (Lu and colleagues, 2022), so select examples systematically, for instance by similarity to the input, and test the effect of their order.
System prompts set the persona and constraints that apply to every turn; keep them stable, so they can be cached and versioned, and put per-request details in the user turn.
Instruction-following weakens when a prompt piles up many constraints, some of them conflicting: test each important constraint with its own checks, and remove rules no case needs.

lessons.title: Reducing hallucinations by design
objectives: Design prompts and pipelines that reduce unsupported claims
Measure hallucination with evaluation cases built for it
key_points: Hallucinations fall when answers are grounded in supplied sources, the model is told it may say it doesn't know, and claims must be backed by a quote or citation.

Chain-of-verification (Dhuliawala and colleagues, 2023) drafts an answer, plans verification questions, answers them independently and revises the draft, which reduced hallucinated facts in their experiments.
Sampling-based checks such as SelfCheckGPT (Manakul and colleagues, 2023) flag claims that vary between independent samples, because facts a model knows tend to be stated consistently.
Constrain outputs where you can, with enums, schemas and tool lookups, and measure the hallucination rate on an evaluation set with known answers and questions that can't be answered.

lessons.title: Prompt optimisation, and when to fine-tune instead
objectives: Run prompt optimisation as a controlled experiment with held-out testing
Choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning for a gap in performance
key_points: Optimise prompts like any experiment: fix the evaluation set and metric, change one thing at a time, run the whole set, and keep a change only if the improvement is larger than the noise.

Tuning on the cases you report overfits the prompt to them: tune on a development set, confirm once on a held-out test set, and compare versions with paired tests such as McNemar's or a paired bootstrap.

Prompt optimisation can be automated, with a model proposing revisions from the failures or frameworks such as DSPy compiling prompts and examples against a metric, but the result still needs held-out testing.

Match the adaptation to the gap: prompting for behaviour you can describe, retrieval for knowledge that changes or must be cited, and fine-tuning for consistent format, style or domain behaviour at scale, or to let a smaller, cheaper model do the job.

Fine-tuning isn't a reliable way to add facts, and it needs labelled data, evaluation and hosting; parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA cut its cost, as Fine-Tuning Open Language Models with LoRA covers in depth.

"""Pick a prompt version from recorded evaluation runs without fooling yourself: development and test splits,
paired comparisons with a bootstrap interval and McNemar's test, and the cost of each version.

runs.csv holds, for each case and prompt version, whether the answer was correct and its output tokens
(made-up runs). v0 is the baseline, v1 adds chain-of-thought, v2 adds few-shot examples, and v3 adds both plus
rules written while looking at the development failures. Run: python optimise.py
"""

import csv
from collections import defaultdict

import numpy as np
from statsmodels.stats.contingency_tables import mcnemar

EXAMPLE_OUTPUT_RATE = 5.00  # dollars per million output tokens: an EXAMPLE rate, not a real price
EXAMPLE_TOKENS_PER_S = 50  # an EXAMPLE generation speed


def load(path="runs.csv"):
    runs = defaultdict(dict)  # (split, variant) -> {case: (correct, tokens)}
    with open(path, newline="") as f:
        for r in csv.DictReader(f):
            runs[r["split"], r["variant"]][r["case"]] = (int(r["correct"]), int(r["output_tokens"]))
    return runs


def accuracy(results):
    return float(np.mean([c for c, _ in results.values()]))


def paired_bootstrap(a, b, n_resamples=10_000, seed=0):
    """95% interval for accuracy(b) - accuracy(a), resampling cases (the same cases for both)."""
    cases = sorted(a)
    diff = np.array([b[c][0] - a[c][0] for c in cases], dtype=float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = diff[rng.integers(0, len(diff), size=(n_resamples, len(diff)))].mean(axis=1)
    return tuple(np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5]))


def mcnemar_p(a, b):
    """McNemar's exact test on the cases where exactly one of the two versions is correct."""
    cases = sorted(a)
    # TODO 1: build the 2x2 table [[both right, only a right], [only b right, both wrong]] and return
    #         mcnemar(table, exact=True).pvalue
    return 1.0


def main():
    runs = load()
    variants = sorted({v for _, v in runs})
    print(f"{'version':<8}{'dev':>6}{'test':>6}{'tokens':>8}{'$/1k req':>10}{'seconds':>9}")
    for v in variants:
        tokens = np.mean([t for _, t in runs["test", v].values()])
        print(f"{v:<8}{accuracy(runs['dev', v]):>6.2f}{accuracy(runs['test', v]):>6.2f}{tokens:>8.0f}"
              f"{tokens * 1000 / 1e6 * EXAMPLE_OUTPUT_RATE:>10.2f}{tokens / EXAMPLE_TOKENS_PER_S:>9.1f}")
    best_dev = max(variants, key=lambda v: accuracy(runs["dev", v]))
    print(f"Best on dev: {best_dev}")
    for v in variants[1:]:
        low, high = paired_bootstrap(runs["test", "v0"], runs["test", v])
        print(f"test, {v} vs v0: difference {accuracy(runs['test', v]) - accuracy(runs['test', 'v0']):+.3f}, "
              f"95% CI {low:+.3f} to {high:+.3f}, McNemar p = {mcnemar_p(runs['test', 'v0'], runs['test', v]):.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""The system under test: a small retrieval-augmented support chatbot for Bluebell Broadband (fictional).

python chatbot.py --demo shows what retrieval finds for the seed queries (no API key needed).
python chatbot.py "your question" answers it (needs ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and CLAUDE_MODEL).
"""

import json
import sys

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

SYSTEM = ("You are Bluebell Broadband's support assistant. Answer only from the articles provided, in at most three "
          "short sentences, politely and plainly, and give the customer a clear next step. If the articles don't "
          "cover the question, say you can't help with that here and suggest contacting the support team.")

with open("kb.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    KB = json.load(f)
VECTORIZER = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
MATRIX = VECTORIZER.fit_transform(a["title"] + ". " + a["text"] for a in KB)


def retrieve(question, k=2):
    scores = cosine_similarity(VECTORIZER.transform([question]), MATRIX)[0]
    ranked = sorted(range(len(KB)), key=lambda i: (-scores[i], i))[:k]
    return [KB[i] for i in ranked if scores[i] > 0]


def build_prompt(question, articles):
    body = "\n".join(f'<article id="{a["id"]}">{a["text"]}</article>' for a in articles) or "(no articles found)"
    return f"<articles>\n{body}\n</articles>\n\n<question>{question}</question>"


def call_model(system, prompt):

    reply = client.messages.create(model=os.environ["CLAUDE_MODEL"], max_tokens=1024, system=system,

    return "".join(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")

    articles = retrieve(question)

def bootstrap_ci(values, n_resamples=10_000, seed=0):
    values = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    means = values[rng.integers(0, len(values), size=(n_resamples, len(values)))].mean(axis=1)
    return np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])


def report(results):
    lines = ["# Evaluation report", "", "| Criterion | Pass rate | 95% CI |", "|---|---|---|"]
    for name in CRITERIA:
        passed = [r["verdicts"][name] == "pass" for r in results]
        low, high = bootstrap_ci(passed)
        lines.append(f"| {name} | {np.mean(passed):.2f} | {low:.2f} to {high:.2f} |")
    labelled = [r for r in results if "human_accuracy" in r]
    agree = np.mean([r["human_accuracy"] == r["verdicts"]["accuracy"] for r in labelled])
    lines += ["", f"Judge vs human labels on accuracy: {agree:.2f} agreement on {len(labelled)} answers.", "",
              "## Failures", ""]
    for r in results:
